status: UNPUBLISHED partial editorial/art draft; not registered in app
sourceReview: Read all bundled BSB Psalm 22, Matthew 27, John 19 and Hebrews 2 before drafting. John 19:24 explicitly connects the dividing of garments with Scripture; Hebrews 2:12 uses the assembly proclamation in its account of Jesus and His brothers. Keep those later contexts distinct from an unspecified original occasion. Read verse 21 through its final declaration of an answer and verse 24 alongside the opening cry.

verses.title: Under their stare
verses.heading: Bodily vulnerability is exposed to gloating eyes
verses.meaning: The speaker can count every bone while others stare and gloat. The line carries forward the physical distress of verses 14–16 and the public humiliation described earlier. Its force lies in the sufferer’s exposure and the onlookers’ lack of compassion. It does not give a diagnosis, explain a cause of illness, or invite readers to inspect a suffering body for themselves. The anonymous clothed figure in the artwork represents vulnerability without making a spectacle of it. Read alongside verse 24, the cruel stare of the onlookers contrasts with the attention that the psalm later affirms God gives to the afflicted.
verses.contextTitle: From wounds to the loss of clothing
verses.context: Verse 16 names surrounding opponents and wounds; verse 17 adds their gloating stare. Verse 18 then describes clothing divided among them. This sequence intensifies the sufferer’s vulnerability without identifying a particular original event.
explore: I can count all my bones
The severe bodily language belongs to the lament’s account of distress. It should be heard with care rather than turned into a medical reconstruction.
They stare and gloat
The onlookers’ attention offers no help. The text gives readers reason to consider the difference between looking at suffering and responding with compassion.
verses.reflect: When someone is vulnerable, what kind of attention preserves their dignity? What would help you offer that attention without making their pain a spectacle?
verses.alt: A weary fully clothed adult sits beneath an olive tree while distant onlookers remain apart in an imagined courtyard.

verses.title: Clothing divided
verses.heading: The speaker’s garments become objects for others to claim
verses.meaning: The opponents divide the speaker’s garments and cast lots for the clothing. The possessions are treated as available to others while the sufferer remains at the center of the lament. The verse does not describe the objects used for the lots or explain the original event, so the artwork’s unmarked pebbles are only symbolic. John 19:23–24 later describes soldiers dividing Jesus’ garments and casting lots for His tunic, explicitly connecting their action with Scripture. Matthew 27:35 also reports garment division by lots. Those later accounts illuminate Christian reading without supplying an invented scene from David’s life.
verses.contextTitle: A line explicitly recalled in John’s Gospel
verses.context: The loss of clothing follows the onlookers’ stare and precedes the renewed appeal of verse 19. John 19:24 quotes this line within its crucifixion account; distinguish that explicit connection from a claim that every detail of the psalm’s original occasion is known.
explore: My garments
The first-person possession keeps the sufferer’s loss visible. The objects are not detached curiosities or an invitation to focus on a method of chance.
Cast lots
The psalm states the action but not its mechanics. The painting’s cloth and smooth stones evoke the line without claiming archaeological or historical precision.
John 19:24
The Gospel explicitly quotes the garment line in its account of the soldiers. Read the surrounding narrative as well as the quoted words.
verses.reflect: What can be lost when people treat another person’s belongings as though that person no longer matters? How might care restore a sense of dignity?
verses.alt: An ivory cloak and sage tunic rest on a low stone bench with a few unmarked pebbles nearby in olive shade.

verses.title: O my Strength, come quickly
verses.heading: The prayer returns from describing danger to directly asking for help
verses.meaning: But You turns the speaker’s attention from the surrounding opponents toward the LORD. The request that God not be far repeats the concern of verse 11, now sharpened by the distress that has followed. Calling God my Strength is especially moving beside the spent strength of verse 15. The speaker asks urgently for help rather than claiming to feel strong already. The line offers a short form of prayer for need, not a rule that sufferers must display confidence before receiving care. Its urgency is preserved even though the poem will soon name an answer.
verses.contextTitle: A renewed appeal after the description of distress
verses.context: Verses 12–18 describe threats, physical distress and humiliation. Verse 19 begins a concentrated plea that continues through verses 20–21. The request for nearness reaches back to both the opening cry and verse 11.
explore: But You, O LORD
The change returns to direct address after the account of what opponents do. It does not report that the danger has ended.
My Strength
The speaker’s dependence is voiced from weakness. The rock in the artwork is an artistic symbol and is not a rock mentioned in this verse.
Come quickly
The request leaves urgency audible within prayer. Readers need not replace an immediate need with language that pretends they are already at ease.
verses.reflect: If you could ask for one concrete form of help right now, what would it be? Who could hear that request alongside your prayer?
verses.alt: An anonymous adult kneels beside a weathered limestone rock at a ravine entrance with hands open in appeal.

verses.title: My precious life
verses.heading: The plea names a life worth rescuing amid lethal danger
verses.meaning: The speaker asks for the rescue of soul and precious life from sword and wild dogs. The paired phrases hold the endangered person at the center of the prayer. Precious life gives a different note from the humiliation voiced earlier as a worm: the sufferer’s life matters even when others treat it with contempt. The sword and dogs express the threat, but the verse does not identify an original attacker or give permission to retaliate. Its action is an appeal for deliverance. The artwork keeps the weapon sheathed and the dogs distant as a symbolic response to danger, rather than a reconstruction of violence.
verses.contextTitle: The animals of threat return in a request for rescue
verses.context: Verse 16 described dogs surrounding the speaker; verse 20 now asks for deliverance from their power. Verse 21 continues the plea with lion and wild oxen. These returning images connect the appeal with the earlier account of encirclement.
explore: Deliver my soul
The request is directed to God for rescue. It is not an instruction for the reader to take vengeance on a perceived opponent.
My precious life
The phrase names the value of the life at risk. It should be read alongside the speaker’s earlier language of humiliation without endorsing contempt.
verses.reflect: What helps you remember that a vulnerable life is precious? How could that conviction shape your response to someone who feels threatened or dismissed?
verses.alt: A sheathed sword lies on pale rocky ground while wary wild dogs stand at a distance beyond an empty path.

verses.title: You have answered me!
verses.heading: The plea reaches an explicit declaration of an answer
verses.meaning: The verse begins as a plea for rescue from the lion’s mouth and the horns of wild oxen, returning to the threatening animal imagery. It ends with the striking declaration that God has answered the speaker. That ending must remain visible: the poem is turning toward the public praise of verses 22–31. The line does not tell how the answer arrived, identify a rescuer, or describe a miraculous escape to illustrate literally. Its shift also does not make the preceding anguish unreal. The whole lament gives space to both the long cry and the answer now proclaimed, without promising every reader the same timetable.
verses.contextTitle: The turning point within a single verse
verses.context: The requests of verses 19–21 culminate in the BSB’s explicit final exclamation, You have answered me! Verse 22 then promises proclamation in the assembly. Read both parts of verse 21 rather than stopping at its danger imagery.
explore: The mouth of the lion
The plea recalls verse 13’s lion comparison. The animal imagery carries the earlier danger into the final request for rescue.
You have answered me!
The declaration marks a change in the poem. The newly open horizon in the painting symbolizes this turn without inventing the way the answer occurred.
verses.reflect: If you have received help after a difficult wait, what part of the earlier struggle still deserves to be heard? How would you tell both parts honestly?
verses.alt: A shadowed ravine opens toward a sunlit olive valley, with a distant lion and wild oxen separated from an empty path.

verses.title: Praise in the assembly
verses.heading: The speaker promises to share God’s name among the gathered community
verses.meaning: After naming an answer, the speaker promises to proclaim God’s name to brothers and praise Him in the assembly. The lament’s voice now turns toward a community that can hear the testimony. The verse does not specify a building, order of service, or particular gathering to reconstruct. Hebrews 2:11–12 later uses this line in its account of Jesus, who is not ashamed to call those He sanctifies brothers. That later Christian use should be read in its own surrounding argument while the psalm’s movement from solitary anguish toward shared praise remains clear. The anonymous gathering in the artwork is symbolic, not a portrait of Jesus or David.
verses.contextTitle: An answered cry becomes a promise of public praise
verses.context: Verse 21 ends with an answer; verse 22 promises proclamation; verse 23 calls the community to praise. Hebrews 2:12 recalls the assembly line after speaking of Jesus and His brothers. Keep that later use distinct from an invented original scene.
explore: I will proclaim
The speaker’s intended response is to tell others of God’s name. The promise follows the answer without erasing the distress that came before.
In the assembly
The movement is toward shared praise. The setting and listening people in the watercolor are artistic choices rather than details supplied by this verse.
Hebrews 2:12
Read the quoted line with verses 9–18, where suffering, family language and help are developed around Jesus. The connection is more than an isolated matching phrase.
verses.reflect: What experience of help would you like to share with people who can listen carefully? What would let your account include gratitude without hiding the hard parts?
verses.alt: An anonymous adult shares with a small listening assembly in an open olive courtyard, standing among peers.

verses.title: Honor Him together
verses.heading: Those who revere the LORD are called into shared praise
verses.meaning: The call addresses those who fear the LORD, descendants of Jacob and offspring of Israel, inviting praise, honor and reverence. These repeated appeals widen the speaker’s promised proclamation into the community’s response. Jacob is a named ancestor in this address, not someone described as present at an event. The verse’s fear belongs with honoring and revering God; it is not the mockers’ intimidation earlier in the poem. The following verse gives a reason for the call: God has attended to the afflicted person’s cry. Shared praise is thus connected to care for the person whose suffering the lament has made audible.
verses.contextTitle: A call to praise followed by its reason
verses.context: Verse 22 promises praise in the assembly; verse 23 calls others to join; verse 24 begins For and explains the attention given to the afflicted. Later verses extend the horizon beyond this community toward the nations and future generations.
explore: Praise, honor, revere
The three invitations reinforce one another. They call for a shared response in the setting of the poem’s turn toward praise.
Descendants of Jacob
The ancestor’s name locates the community being addressed. It does not supply a new biographical scene or identify a model for any figure in the painting.
verses.reflect: When gratitude is shared in a community, whose experience can easily be overlooked? How might honoring God include making room for the afflicted person’s voice?
verses.alt: An anonymous gathering of adults and seated elders shares quiet reverent praise on a stone terrace beside an olive grove.

verses.title: The afflicted cry is heard
verses.heading: The speaker affirms attention instead of contempt or a hidden face
verses.meaning: For introduces the reason for the community’s praise: God has not despised the afflicted person’s torment or hidden His face, but has attended to the cry for help. This answers the mockers’ contempt and stands in powerful conversation with the opening question about abandonment. The declaration must not be used to scold someone still living with that question. The psalm itself first gave the cry room to be heard and did not explain the pain away. Its closing confidence affirms regard for the afflicted; it does not give readers a timetable or a guarantee that every hardship will end in the same way.
verses.contextTitle: The reason for praise reaches back to the opening cry
verses.context: Verse 24 follows the invitation to praise and explains it through God’s attention to the afflicted. Read it beside verses 1–2 and the ridicule of verses 6–8. The speaker’s testimony now gives a response to those earlier experiences without denying they were painful.
explore: Has not despised
The declaration contrasts with human scorn earlier in the lament. The afflicted person is not dismissed as unworthy of attention.
Has attended to his cry
The answer now proclaimed concerns the cry that opened the poem. The artwork’s human listener symbolizes compassionate attention and does not portray God as a human body.
verses.reflect: What would it mean to listen to an afflicted person without dismissing their cry? What kind of attention would you welcome when you are the one hurting?
verses.alt: Two anonymous adults sit at the same level beneath an olive tree, one weary and the other listening attentively.
